newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OLYMPICS-SYDNEY ORGANISERS CAUGHT IN BED TAX ROW.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-SYDNEY ORGANISERS CAUGHT IN BED TAX ROW.

text.p: Sydney Olympic organisers warned on Monday that a worsening row between city hotels and the state government was putting at risking lucrative sponsorship deals worth several hundred million dollars.
Organising committee vice-president John Coates said potential sponsors would consider walking away because of a lack of guaranteed hotel accommodation during the 2000 Sydney Games.
"We have not had a bigger problem than this since we started organising the Games," Coates told a news conference.
Major hotels in Sydney's central business district have suspended negotiations with Olympic organisers in protest at a proposed 10-percent bed tax on hotel room rates.
The New South Wales state government is planning to introduce the tax from September to help pay for the massive infrastructure costs in staging the Games.
Olympic organisers have secured little more than one-third of the 25,000 hotel rooms they need in central Sydney to satisfy their requirements, Coates said.
Unless the dispute is settled, the Sydney Organising Committee for the Olympic Games would be unable to guarantee accommodation as part of sponsorship packages, Coates said.
Either the contracts would have to be renegotiated at lower rates or potential sponsors may "walk away and...not want to sign," Coates said.
More than A$300 million (US$225 million) sponsorship revenue was at risk, Coates said, adding: "It is a very serious threat and it is very damaging to our marketing department."
He said the growing row over hotel beds was making Sydney's preparations "look inept" in the eyes of the international community.
The Olympic body was prepared to act as a mediator in the hope of finding a compromise between the major hotels and the government, Coates said.
But he said New South Wales premier Bob Carr had indicated privately that he would consider introducing future legislation to commandeer the necessary number of hotel rooms.
"I would prefer that the Olympic movement was not party to that kind of legislation," Coates said, adding that Games organisers needed hoteliers' goodwill and not just their rooms.
